reference.title: Pelvic Tilt
reference.listing: Page could not be read here (gymvisual.com is blocked by the proxy); the movement is taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice.

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you flatten the back and tilt the pelvis; inhale as you release.
breathing.cadence: About 5 s per rep with a short hold

prescription.tempo: 1.2 s tilt, 1.5 s hold, 1.3 s release
prescription.frequency: Daily as a warm-up or rehab drill
prescription.progression: Longer holds, then add marching or a glute bridge from the tilted position

cues.text: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip width apart, arms by your sides.
Breathe out and gently flatten your low back into the mat by rolling the pelvis back (tailbone curls up slightly).
Hold for a couple of seconds; keep the buttocks on the mat and the ribs relaxed.
Breathe in and let the pelvis roll back to neutral, with a small natural gap under the low back.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the buttocks into a bridge
mistakes.fix: Keep the buttocks resting on the mat; the movement is small.

mistakes.mistake: Pushing with the feet or legs only
mistakes.fix: Draw the belly in and let the abdominals do the tilting.

mistakes.mistake: Jamming the head into the mat

kinematics.norm: Small posterior tilt, about 5-15 degrees (clinical opinion)
Low back flattens toward the mat (Drysdale 2004)
Slow, with a 1-2 s hold (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #11667, Pelvic Tilt, video (movement reference; page not readable here)
Drysdale, Earl and Hertel 2004, surface EMG of the abdominal muscles during pelvic-tilt and abdominal-hollowing exercises (J Athl Train 39(1):32-36)
Escamilla et al. 2006, electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training (Phys Ther 86(5):656-671; PubMed 16649890)
Oliva-Lozano and Muyor 2020, core muscle activity during physical fitness exercises: a systematic review (Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(12):4306)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
A gentle movement: it should not hurt. Stop and get advice if it brings on back or leg pain.
modify: A folded towel under the head if the neck is uncomfortable.
Do it standing with the back against a wall if lying down is uncomfortable.
Pregnancy, postpartum or diastasis recti: get cleared first, and avoid long supine work later in pregnancy.
regressions: Hands on the belly to feel the abdominals draw in.
progressions: Hold the tilt while marching one foot up at a time.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the front of the pelvis up toward the ribs and flattens the low back into the mat; in Drysdale 2004 the posterior pelvic tilt drew more rectus abdominis and external oblique activity than abdominal hollowing.
muscleNotes.glute_max_r: Gluteus maximus helps roll the pelvis back (posterior tilt) without lifting the buttocks off the mat (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_max_l: Gluteus maximus helps roll the pelvis back (posterior tilt) without lifting the buttocks off the mat (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External obliques assist the tilt and hold the ribs down (Drysdale 2004).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External obliques assist the tilt and hold the ribs down (Drysdale 2004).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: With the feet planted the hamstrings can help draw the pelvis back (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_l: With the feet planted the hamstrings can help draw the pelvis back (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: The lumbar extensors relax and lengthen a little as the low back flattens (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: The lumbar extensors relax and lengthen a little as the low back flattens (clinical opinion).
